description_full: Commercial Metals Company manufactures, recycles, and fabricates steel and metal products, and related materials and services in the United States, Poland, China, and internationally. It operates through three segments: North America Steel Group, Construction Solutions Group, and Europe Steel Group. The company processes and sells ferrous and nonferrous scrap metals. It also offers finished long steel products, including reinforcing bars, merchant bars, light structural and other special sections, and wire rods, as well as semi-finished billets for rerolling and forging applications. In addition, the company provides fabricated rebar used to reinforce concrete; sells and rents construction-related products and equipment; and manufactures and sells strength and armor plates. Further, it sells wire meshes, welded steel mesh, wire rod, cold rolled rebar, cold rolled wire rod, assembled rebar cages and other fabricated rebar by-products. The company was founded in 1915 and is headquartered in Irving, Texas.

financial_summary: Commercial Metals Company is a mid-cap industrials business with a $6.9B market cap on $9.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 11% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $479M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.61× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.4× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.0×.

Shareholder yield of 2.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 8% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.68x).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 10% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 11% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 27% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 36% and a beta of 1.11, it moves roughly with the market.
About $70.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.

val: The stock trades 50% below its DCF fair value of $123, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 47%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $81.35 to $185 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 10.6 vs 24.1, EV/EBITDA 7.8 vs 13.4 and P/FCF 14.3 vs 22.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 19% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 7.0% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The 11 covering analysts target $78.45 on average, 26% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 11% earns above the cost of capital of 8.2%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.01).
It converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.61x.
ROE of 14% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.5% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.4x net debt to EBITDA ($775.7M of cash against $3.4B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.0x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.2% over 3 years, 6.9% over 5 years and 7.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 16%).
At current returns, reinvesting 19% of profits supports about 2.2% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 61.0% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 10% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 7%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.5x, 6.2% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 12, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.8%), and institutions hold 95%.
It returns 2.7% a year to shareholders (1.5% in buybacks and 1.3% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, raising it 7.8% a year over the last five.
people: With about 13,670 employees, each generates about $687K of revenue, 1.9x the Industrials median.
That works out to $35K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.5M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
